title: Mochin DeTzelem, Vol. 13: Questions Are Kelim
subtitle: The world stands on three things: Torah, Avodah and Chassadim.
html:
From Mikraei Kodesh, the Torah writings collected on liorsollyshachar.com.

1, 2, 3, 4:

We remember that questions are kelim for answers. The forgettable part is that when you are given an answer, you have nothing to do with it until you fashion a question around it. That is to say, if you don’t know what you want to know, or you don’t care about the question that holds the answer, then there is nothing for you to do with the Ohr. Flamingo – case in point. We are presented with a Mishnah in Avot. The Olam is Omed on three things: Torah, Avodah and Chassadim. This is an answer, but what is the question?

From the inventory of kelim, we begin with ‘What.’ It is clear that what we are presented with is an anatomy, and we can also observe it is a partial anatomy of a bigger whole. The whole thing is an Olam, and the assumption is that there is a need for an Amidah, i.e. an anatomical component that has the function of being ma’amid the Olam. We are then given a set of three objects, [Torah, Avodah, Chassadim]. Would the assumption be that an Olam can be stood up on the spine of any of these three amudim, i.e. pillars i.e. lines i.e. axes i.e. kavin? That is to say, does every Olam require three kavin in order to stand, or can an Olam stand on one kav, meaning to say, a kav which has the function of regel, that which stands a person up, like we find in the Gemara in Chagigah regarding people who walk using kavin to the Bet HaMikdash during the three regalim, i.e. raglayim, i.e. amudim, i.e. kavin?

We layer How on What and ask: are these three activities which must be done by people populating the Olam? Are these three energies that go into the construction of any given Olam milema’ala? Are these three types of personalities that a societal Olam needs? Are these three components of a singular (v.) Activity? Are these three components of any singular (n.) Object? Our mysteries continue to lie in the ambiguity of the question. Really, what we need to ask is, what are these dichotomous states of Nefilah and Amidah that this set is supposed to affect?

Let’s assume that the Olam is omed on things we do. Let us make that assumption because Torah, Avodah and Chassadim are three mitzvot from a larger set of Taryag mitzvot, and mitzvot concern our activity. The statement would be that of the 613, only three either can hold up the Olam or are necessary to hold up the Olam, both of which are slightly uncomfortable readings because Taryag is a whole human body. A whole human body can withstand some amputation, but even in that marginal case, that’s tolerating a terrible situation. You definitely can’t put a brain, a liver and a pinky finger in a bathtub and let the body proceed as if it’s just another Tuesday1. Be that as it may, the Mishnah would be telling us ‘Adam is ma’amid the Olam, and if he doesn’t do some things, then the Olam is nofel. So, what must he do? Etc.’ The implication of this Mishnah, if it is as we are saying, clues us into the identity of Adam within the system of a universe. We know from the Mishnayot in Taharot that when a material is ma’amid a kli, which is to say that without it the kli would break, the entire kli is called by the identity of the ma’amid. The ma’amid, the capstone as it were, is what holds the entire dome in place. Does that imply that failure in terms of whatever these three mean becomes a failure of Adam as an Adam? More importantly, we need to figure out Why exactly it is that these three cause the world to align with Amidah, and how they address Nefilah.

Chazal explain to us that every structure in the universe shares universal principles of design. Adam nivrah betzelem Elokim is an extension of this concept, as Chazal explain: Adam’s entire body, the whole Taryag, is built yashar with three kavin. Chazal further specify that these three kavin are in fact arranged in a geometry of Left, Right and Center, or in other words, a Kav Yamin, Kav Smol, and a Kav Emtzai2. Chazal go on to add that this geometry is more elemental to reality than we might have thought in assuming the Mishnah is only about Adam. They reveal that really left and right are polarities, and the middle is something of a union between the two. It becomes clear that these polarities are ubiquitous in Torah’s definition of any and all anatomy. Chazal identify the polarity of Kav Yamin with the polarity of Zachrut and Ohr and Chassadim, while Kav Smol is identified with the polarity of Nakvut and Kli and Gvurot. When Ohr and Kli are joined together, a Kav Emtzai emerges called Rachamim, which is the sweetening of the Kli’s lonesome bitterness with the sweet joy of Ohr. Beyond just left and right, whenever you have a ma’ala and mata or an achor and panim, for example, we find an aspect of these two polarities in relation to each other3. So that would make Ohr Panim bechinat Zachrut and Ohr Chozer, i.e. Ohr Achor, bechinat Nukvah, Dinim and Tzimtzumim. There are three kavin showing up in this Mishnah, and the way they are being communicated is through synonyms: Chassadim = Kav Yamin, Avodah = Kav Smol, and Torah = Kav Emtzai. So it turns out that the Mishnah is describing a situation, one of many in the universe, in which three kavin are ma’amid. But it is focusing in on a particular instance, and informing us what the three kavin of that space are.

The question then becomes, first of all, why are these three mitzvot an expression of the three kavin? And then, what is the particular system we are being taught about? When are those the three amudim, and not the three legs of my barstool? Meaning to say, there are many structures that all have three kavin, and not all of them are the same. What is the anatomically complete Olam such that its three kavin are the set we are told in the Mishnah? This is sort of like those children’s games where you have to match the leg to the animal. We are given a leg; what is the animal that stands on it? In other words, not “al shlosha avot” or “al shloshet raglei hashana” or “al kachab” or “al chagat” or “al nahi”, all of which are arranged in the same geometry.

In explaining this Mishnah, Rav Ezra Neuberger said that these three relate to the three categories of narrative: Man versus Man, Man versus Environment, and Man versus Self. He then explained further that these three kinds of narrative are based in the three relationships: Ben Adam LeChavero, Ben Adam LaMakom and Ben Adam LeAtzmo. The depth at which this statement contacts reality is overwhelming. 4

First and foremost, we can now grasp at the Mishnah with the highest maturity achieved thus far with the following kli: What are the three base vectors of relationship within an individual5? The answer is: Torah, Avodah and Chassadim. Really, the Mishnah’s full flow is as follows: The Olam stands with Life; that is what it means to be kayam, namely, to be alive. What is it that we do as nivraim in a world of din, where the Olam is only given life, i.e., Rain, as a response to our Mayin Nukvin? We do Torah, Avodah and Chassadim, which are engagements with the Briah along the three relational axes in alignment with the ubiquitous three kavin as represented by these three mitzvot.

But gufa, that statement itself, that the three kavin are the base vectors of a three-dimensional matrix of relationship, that needs unpacking. Ben Adam LeChavero means you in relation to the social system. The social system is a physical phenomenon, because Yisrael isn’t actually a separated entity. What Kudsha Brich Hu did was make a world where the different shards of a totality are embedded in separated, discrete bodies, which opens the space for a reality of individual personalities, which would be impossible in a space where everyone is integrated. And then, through the development of one’s individuality, one becomes a mature participant within the new entity of the social system that reunifies all the separated pieces into a single whole, within this land of material alienation. The resistance force to cohering as a society demands a revelation of culture against that entropic resistance; there you see the story of sprawling civilization before you, all these cities and artists and economies, all the smells and the sounds one hears and the tears of joy and sorrow in the vastness of skyscraping urbanity, all because people decided long ago simply to live together. The fact that the whole needs to find its seamless connection once again is the best possible setting for friction, because the closer you are to someone and the more they matter to you, the more you need to sand down the roughness of your own individuality to accommodate the differences of an other, and to see them as part of you even if their face makes you want to reject them on sight as an ‘other.’ This is the literary space of Man versus Man, in which the Author Baruch Hu can write and read stories about the struggles and triumphs of interpersonal drama and romance, of community and fraternity, of war and peace.

Ben Adam LaMakom is an interesting phrase, because we don’t often refer to Kudsha Brich Hu as Makom. But He is, in point of fact, the Makom, i.e., Hu Mekomo Shel Olam. The entire information space that exists, and in which we exist, is information He is thinking! This is Man versus Environment, because you are turned outward toward reality, toward the environment which is the space beyond the system’s boundaries, the outside, and are forced to fight with the world around you to see that Kudsha Brich Hu is the only thing behind this façade. Man versus Environment is consequently the space of Tefillah, which is the nexus of personal experience and personal goals and activity which always demands that you daven for what you need. It’s the story of a lone person in a forest, trying to make it from one day to the next without getting eaten, which is a more meaningful story in the metropolitan contexts we live in than any forest setting could provide. In this book, the Author writes stories about individuals, invisible triumphs known only within the intimacy between Adam LaMakom because nobody could see the true inner drama of you versus the universe, and whatever they do see, it’s not the half of it. If it is, check your pulse, you might not be alive. Kav Smol is not a social moment, inasmuch as you aren’t participating in the social system, but it is the least lonely of all these relationships. In the social system, you are forever alienated from the other by the fact that you are in a discrete body. You can’t know what the other person thinks or feels like; you are forever held within the prison of yourself. And when nobody is there, you particularly feel the condition of being the only consciousness around in the universe that you have access to. Wherever you go, that’s where you are, and nobody else can follow you. That is, until you realize that there is Another who does see and understand you, and cares about you personally. This is Tefillah, which is the internalization of Memale Kol Almin, that Kudsha Brich Hu is literally right where you are, and He never left the Chalal for an instant.

The Kav Emtzai is Identity, and is concerned with who you are and how you see. This is why the nose, which is Tiferet, is totally unique to you, to the point that we can identify a person whose corpse is totally mutilated by his nose6 alone! Everyone’s nose is morphogenetically determined by their Da’at, and no two noses are alike. This is Ben Adam LeAtzmo. It’s not obvious to most that this is a relationship at all, but a look under the hood will reveal that what you thought was simply ‘yourself’ is really a zoo, nay, a circus, and the ringmaster is constantly out of breath yelling at the clowns to help him break up a fight between the monkey and the elephant7 who stole its fez because he thought it was a peanut. This is the drama of self-actualization, and it is certainly a relationship. The context that nurtures this relationship most, and a context which is extremely important for any avodah to actually take place, is solitude. You can never discover your own voice in a crowd, and even when you know your own voice, it becomes dulled by being among people regardless of whether the people are doing anything bad, just by virtue of their being other people, you are dulled8. Your own voice and your own will are what develop as you mature; they are a product of mochin degadlut. Your war with yourself is through Torah. R Ezra explained in the course of the point he was making that no matter what you are struggling with – alienation from community, identity struggles, trouble waking up in the morning – it will all come out along the path towards fighting for the mitzvah of limud hatorah, through all the walls you need to break just to sit in front of a gemara and learn in tranquil joie de vivre. If you are not male and are under the false impression that Torah is an inapplicable category to you as a woman, or in the more likely case that you are a man, and feel that Torah is not something you understand how to connect to (and yet have managed to get to this point in the piece): Ohr Torah is chochmah, and chochmah is enayim, and what Torah comes down to is not a volume of repertoire but your vision. Identity is vision. You are vision. Your substance and function are being an object of experience, the consciousness and perception of the universe. That is what the neshamot are, objects of visual experience that emerge as wholes from otiot, while the downstream products of personality, of the materiality dressing the ‘self’ or anything else – that’s all just infrastructure around what you really areג. But fundamentally, the Neshama is an object of vision. Torah is vision, and that is what one aims to cultivate in engagement with Torah. This is true regardless of whether you are a man or otherwise: the mitzvah of limud hatorah is to be davuk to light, which is a visual event, and however you learn to see is engagement with Torah, provided what you are learning to see is Torah, which is never constrained to Gefet9.

So to put it together, we are being taught that our job is to engage in the process of bringing life to the world10. The Kav Yamin is the polarity of Ohr, Zachrut. Ben Adam LeChavero is expressed as Chassadim. The nature of Ohr is to spread, to be noten. The Kav Smol is the polarity of mekabel, nekevah, kli, to hold, shape and define, defined antonymously to the Yamin which is by definition boundless giving and extension, filling all the space equally. Without Gvurot Geshamim, the lifewater of the sky would be a homogeneously distributed vapor. How is vision of the world formed through the prism of Chassadim? Perception on the plane of Ben Adam LeChavero is a question that asks how to connect with an other. Sometimes that means how to give them help or engender a relationship, which is a goal in and of itself in an olam where Yisrael needs to be united keechad for the geulah to come, just as in the moment of Keish Echad Belev Echad at Matan Torah11. Sometimes, though, the very kli of perception of the other as an other who is worthy of perception and dignification is itself the gift. To do Chassadim with a kli means to give a kli that has no boundaries, to give an ear and an eye that doesn’t go anywhere if the other is in some way different than you are used to. This is the kli of total, unconditional acceptance. That is the boundlessness of Ben Adam LeChavero. So many find it easy to convince themselves that the avodah is done when their material tzedakah flows boundlessly, but the kli given to another might still have the boundaries of festering bigotry and cynicism that look at all others in a twisted and bitter light, as extractors and opportunistic and lazy and dumber and less human, all of which are the opposite of Chassadim. You can never be a ba’al chesed from a distance.

Relationship is emergent when two systems have what to do with one another. I am baking a cake, you sell flour, I buy your flour. We now have a relationship. This is why the merchant is called a chenveni from the shoresh ‘Chen12’, Middat Yosef HaTzadik, Middat Yesod. The Vav is a Tzadik, the mechaber between the makom of Yud Kei and the Chalal. Yesod is the Ohr Ne’erav, the Alloy, that separates between the pargod of binah and gvurah in the instantaneous making of Olam HaMalbush. Yesod is the common ground between the others. The Ohr of the five Chassadim, Chagat Netzach and Hod, all flows into the kli of Yesod, which despite a haara of its own doesn’t have an Ohr of its own13. It is the nexus point where the resources flow to Yosef and he distributes to the kingdom, literally the melucha.

Commerce is a level of relationship, but the magnetism on that paradigm is necessity. Gemilut Chassadim is deeper. Gamal means to repay, as in Havaya Gamal Alai, or Gamalta Ra’ah if you paid back good with evil. It means to wean, to develop the other into individuality. It means to be involved in a situation until its completion14, to bring the child to the completion of the stage, to close the circuit of a debt relationship (i.e. to pay back). Gemilut Chassadim means to do Chassadim that are complete, fully giving to the other and fully extending yourself. It means doing a chesed that is oriented towards the other, not chesed to create debt dependency, which is the opposite of gemilut; it means to help the other in their journey towards ripening and actualization, for them, so they become independent. You do not give a man a fish so that he may become dependent on your manipulative dynamic of giving so as to be repaid in emotional labor. You teach a man to fish so that he doesn’t need you anymore. Are you willing to step away after you help? Are you willing to help insofar as they need, and not for your own needs? That is a true relationship of Chassadim. And that’s why R Ezra explained that Kav Yamin is the space for emulating Kudsha Brich Hu al derech Ma Hu Rachum Af Ata. What is the dimyon exactly? Because on the horizontal paradigm of Ben Adam LeChavero one thinks and acts in a way that is Zachar, noten, as if one has light. And there is light, but it’s His light, and in orienting towards others as a noten, you become a dimyon of Him, because the true Zachar and Nekevah is Kudsha Brich Hu to us, the collective nekevah. We are never the noten. Tzedakah is always Tzedek, so don’t let it go to your head that you are a Tzadik; you are only Matzdik the Emet, or as we say in Tziduk HaDin15, Baruch Dayan HaEmet. The Dayan is Elokim, ba’al hayecholet vekochot kulam. He has all the energies; your credit card swipes in every movement you make but He is the bank account. Be thankful your card doesn’t get declined, and never make the mistake of thinking that you are the noten, that you are the brilliant businessman. So many people make the mistake of thinking that the dumb luck of being first to market for whatever reason and gaining that marginal advantage which compounds into escape velocity for the company, eventually surfacing as the top in their sector, is a result of kocham veotzem yadam and not the lottery of complex systems16.

By contrast, Avodah is not the opposite of giving oneself. What it means to see the world through the prism of Kav Smol is the vertical geometry of Ben Adam LaMakom, the perception that you don’t have any light of your own, that as much as you are a zachar horizontally, you are bichlalut the nukvah that is let beh migarmeh klum. You are a kli, an Eved that cannot own possessions. The giving of Avodah Zu HaKorbanot is a recognition in relation to everything you have; Avodah SheBalev is becoming an Eved Balev. R Ezra explained that rather than acting like HaShem, in the Kav Smol you talk with HaShem. It’s a conversation. And that conversation of course occurs during tefillah, but the deeper truth is that from within the experience of the world beyond yourself, when you are not transfixed on you or an other, only the world as a place surrounding you on all sides, you experience the modality of tefillah. It’s Kudsha Brich Hu as disclosed through the medium of the entire universe itself, His architecture and curation. This is why the literary category is Man versus Environment. The entire world contorts around you as a place of Personality, and that Personality doesn’t speak but it is resounding. This is the relationship directly to Kudsha Brich Hu that occurs on the polarity of Nukvah and Kli. It is also tefillah, as it happens, that brings down the gvurot geshamim. It is Adam in the reconnaissance of tefillah that causes a magnetism pulling the Chassadim inward toward himself. Tefillah is standing before Kudsha Brich Hu and wanting what you need so much that your stomach clenches and you generate a black hole of ratzon pulling all the light inward. In a more mature stage, that ratzon is for the yichud of Kudsha Brich Hu uShechinte, for tikun gamur, but even in the more external layers, that operation looks and feels the same. It is kli-ness, ratzon lekabel, even if it isn’t quite yet holding by ratzon lekabel betenai lehashpia.

The idea of relationship presumes two points, and around those points a bipolar sphere of relationship emerges. Counterintuitively, this is the case within oneself. There is the experience of being encased in the warmth of our own presence, in the intimate kodesh kodashim of our inner being, though the two points here are harder to identify. It’s a bit of a stretch from our normal mode of operating, but pause and feel that you are sitting in the place of yourself, your body is warm and keeping you company, you are in your own head and thinking words. Perhaps I’m there with you insofar as these words are an input channel in the feedback loop of your own mind, but this is not the main character; you are. Consider the experience of sitting in front of a gemara and learning. First, you struggle a bit to get into it, being that you are rubbing up against the klipat egoz, but with some inner encouragement that putting your mind in Torah Space is a mitzvah, Ratzon HaShem, and will be gorem yichud, you break through. You might have a bit of a debate, because you are tired for legitimate reasons etc., but eventually all the participating voices in the discussion are thrown to the sidelines and the gemara becomes the thing that fills the space of your mind. The gemara eclipses your inner dialogue. You are nearly eclipsed by the gemara, but not quite17. At the end of the day, there is a focal point of the limud, and that focal point is the main character, not the gemara itself. You are the object of vision that is undergoing a change of vision, that is encountering a new piece of information that is being understood on its own terms, compared with what you currently assume; perhaps you remember and flip around to that other gemara that was itching you, and you confirm your suspicions. This new gemara in fact challenges your worldview, challenges your being. Are you going to take this offense sitting down? Of course not! Or perhaps you will be sitting down, but you definitely won’t go down without a fight. Whatever the outcome, you have changed, and you are that object that changes. You are a thing, an irreducible being which is the yardstick by which new Torah is measured in relation to your current tfisah of Torah. New Torah changes how you see the world, migrates you to a different world than the one you thought you existed in, and demands of you to change yourself to conform to the new demands of this world, halachic or otherwise. If you don’t have any existence of your own, how can you feel an existential crisis when you find out midway through Masechet Shabbat that there is a Tana who barely holds of muktze at all which you might have grown up thinking was of the gimel chamurot! This is where the line comes from that if you don’t die from a kasha you don’t live from a teretz. Ohr is life, and if you don’t have a kli, because you are shallow and don’t care about the information, then you can’t hold that Ohr. If you aren’t already a fully-fledged individuality that is personally invested in understanding Torah, motivated by the reality that it hasn’t already all been said and done, and definitely not by you, then you have no hope of retaining the information. This is why Ish is prat lekatan, mochin degadlut, an individuality utterly unique and irreplaceable, Ze Moshe HaIsh who is never going to be replaced by anybody, and who lives in everybody who grows into themselves as a mature lomed torah. You change and work through your identity, personality building, emotional control etc., all through the war to move closer to the inner sanctum of reality as it is. Those who stand complacently on the outside of reality and have no desire to move deeper are those people we see as the complacent masses who will remain unchanged with time, who will be the exact same person in another decade, going through the same ossified cycles around nothing, albeit with some more unearned white hair. A true zaken is ze shekana chochmah, as we find in Kiddushin. But those who have not been kone chochmah are those who never desired to enter deeper into reality, who were fine outside the center, who were fine all the way in the corners, as far as they could get from the fire in the center of the machane. In other words, these are the yoshvei hakranot, from keren, meaning corner, who have no perot in olam haze nor do they have keren in olam haba, keren meaning principle, but also meaning the antlers of mythic achievement of coming to olam haze and finding their way back home to reality despite.

Nobody expected that; they all thought it was impossible, but you didn’t think it was, why would you have? And so you did it, and you made it look easy, but you will find it was nearly impossible. When you pass, you will see it was an Everest, while the yetzer hara will cry because it looks like an ant hill. That keren, the karnei ohr, is the keter of Torah, available to everybody, and thus implicating everybody who remains a blooming wallflower of darkness in the corners. Those on a journey toward the center will find so much garbage burned away, will find so much new growth, new warmth, and thus are always forced to reinvent themselves. This is why the migration inward toward reality, only through Torah which is the territory of reality, is the process that makes you and finds you and turns you into who you really are; as an object of vision, who you are is your chelek in Torah, your real estate in the Taryag of Yisrael, merumaz in the Torah’s 600,000 otiot, shorshei neshama, where you are merumaz in a place nobody else occupies. Either remain with the nameless demographic in the corners or find your name among the shemot of Atzilut, your identity, your true self, in the olam of Ohr in the center18. It goes without saying that any Yisrael (the full set of which are the twin partzufim of Zachar and Nekevah with a full koma of Abya to themselves) is by definition one whose soul demands a development, a deepening of the relationship between them and their self, correcting and advancing their model of what the world is.

Kav Emtzai, R Ezra explained, is the relationship of learning with HaShem across from you. This is the enchanting thing about limud hatorah, that Kudsha Brich Hu extends a direct channel of information into your feedback loop of limud hatorah, that special moment when understanding strikes through from the outside, the yagata umatzata, the thing you found, the hashavat aveida, that kiss on the forehead of yeshakeni meneshikot pihu for all the yegia. And even with a chavrusa of flesh and blood, that is not a social experience in the space of Chassadim because you aren’t your selves; there is a third thing up in the middle between you, the sugya, which is being codeveloped without any regard as to the identity of the chavrusa. It’s two people who are mevatel themselves for a couple hours and Kudsha Brich Hu becomes the shared focal point, whether or not the individuals choose to recognize it as such.

As we said, Chazal teach us that the middle kav is the union of the two poles. The duality, i.e., the space of emulating Kudsha Brich Hu, in one’s giving of light to others, in one’s respect and regard for others, and the space of talking with Kudsha Brich Hu, realizing the light isn’t your own, are unified in the space of Emtza. In the development and transformation of your self and thus your rendering of the world you live in as a space of reality, you realize that Memale Kol Almin penetrates the entire horizontal fabric of Ben Adam LeChavero, you see at once that the light isn’t yours and that it is being given to others only through you. In learning Torah and becoming acquainted with the sight of reality, you see others as possessed of eyes that illuminate with life and subjectivity behind them just as much as you, life coming from the same place yours does, which is not your own strength, and because of that, you are completely open to accept and hear the other person, because there is no threat to your identity either in association or in the risk of being bettered, because there is no such thing as madrega in an olam of Ovi, which is the metukan perception of reality.

It is for this reason that we find life in the center. Keter is the root of Ratzon and the Ayin that materializes in the individual has identity in Ani. Keter is the mamshak between the life in the olam above and the kelim of the olam below. It is what becomes Malchut. And Da’at, the perfect balance in metabolizing complexity through the digestive system of svara, is really just Keter. And we know that below Da’at is Tiferet, perfect balance once again, the Tzadik, which also refers to below Tiferet, namely Yesod, the place that collects all the energies, and gives finally into the bottom of the Kav Emtzai, Malchut, the Nukvah of Kav Smol and the Noten of Kav Yamin, because netina can only happen through gvurot. As a kli, it is mashpia.

The Komarna asks in Nesiv Mitzvosecha: what is the point of tefillah? The implications of this question are massive, because if we empty our ears of the cotton numbness resisting the relitigating of things we think we know, we realize that Tefillah, an entire third of this universal anatomy, an activity that consumes many a waking hour, is in fact deeply mysterious. The answer cannot be found in the red herrings of idiotic translation by those who understand nothing and see nothing through the thickness of academic dust. ‘Praying’, ‘supplicating’, ‘meditating’, ‘liturgy’ – these are all byzantine inanities. The identification of what tefillah is has the consequence of shaping how we approach the action of tefillah. It is clearly a mental and verbal action, so the mind is being told to do a thing, sort of like how the mitzvah of limud hatorah is telling you to do a thing with your mind, and is fulfilled when your mind is doing the thing. But in tefillah there is a verbal component. So, what is this action of cerebral externalization meant to accomplish? What is the soul of thought that is supposed to be invested and embedded within the vapor of one’s verbal tefillah? Meaning, we look at the words of tefillah when our tefillah is structured19 and try to understand their meaning, but their meaning is surely to be understood not in its native context but as words smuggled from their native context and arranged in a tefillah. So, what is this activity that then manifests in a ‘Siddur’ (from seder meaning system)?

The Komarna reveals: the activity of tefillah is to internalize Memale Kol Almin, that Kudsha Brich Hu never really left the Chalal. Of course, we can now understand why this theme of internalizing Memale Kol Almin through conversation is one of the three threads that progress through the Briah, because the point of returning to Yud Kei Yud Kei is that we arrive with the kelim to fully internalize as an Ohr Penimi the Ohr Bli Gvul that wasn’t possible to be masig on the level of Yud Kei Vav Kei. But really the one-on-one conversation in which one internalizes Memale Kol Almin through the modality of Avdut, tefillah, is actually a leftward expression of the middle kav, the kav of consciousness and identity, the kav of Torah, your thoughts. Torah is how you see the world; Torah teaches that HaShem is Echad. Granted, the Torah of Atzilut teaches that best, but all Torah is invariably the education of Echad. In tefillah that understanding goes from the head out through speech in conversation.

The goyim have fleeced Yisrael on multiple occasions, and in each occasion Yisrael are made to feel as if those stolen objects were never in fact their intellectual property and worse, it would be a chukat haakum to reclaim that intellectual property! This is a tragedy, because those stolen objects are at times central to our avodah, and Yisrael must steal them back, and dust off the nonsense of warp and dream toxins that inevitably accumulated while away. One of these properties is a mode of being which the goyim have stolen and repackaged as ‘meditation’. Kavana is not something one can trip on by accident; it is something that has to be worked on and cultivated, it is a space one enters only on purpose. It is a space that requires hachana beforehand, as all the sefarim on tefillah inform us. What does that look like? How does one do the activity of being mechaven, mechaven from kivun which is alignment with the space one wants to enter20?

We use the term Tefillah BeKavana, about which we say, Tefillah Bli Kavana is like a Guf without a Neshama. Where does Kavana come from? It comes from the middle column. How can you be mechaven to HaShem if you don’t exist, if you aren’t a person in the world with a vantage point and a subjectivity from which to look at the Other and say ‘I See You’? And how can one converse in a way that assumes HaShem Echad and Memale Kol Almin if one never spent the time in Torah to understand what world one lives in, the world to which tefillah is a reaction? Tefillah is an externalization of what one sees. You can’t talk about what you don’t see21. So open your eyes! How? With limud hatorah, and only with limud hatorah.

But the Kav Emtzai also turns into the Kav Yamin. Whereas in the case of Kav Smol that took the form of Dibur, the feedback loop of Chassadim is seeing the world and acting on it. You can’t do chesed with the empty vapor of “You got this boss, I believe in you, no pain no gain, it’s grind o’clock amiright gym rats?” You actually have to be porek the masa, i.e. help him take the saddlebags off of the donkey.

It turns out the three we thought were parallel vertically are also three horizontally22, the progression of Machshava, Dibur and Ma’aseh. Where does this come from? As in, what is the deeper anatomy that is the umbrella klal becoming both vertical and horizontal polarities? We know that there are always three kelim. Meaning, in the Yud Kei Vav Kei, we have the first Ot which is two bechinot, Keter and Chochmah, which always stay outside, followed by three kelim, heh vav heh, in which the Ohr Penimi is nichnas inside. These are the Nefesh (Heh), Ruach (Vav), Neshama (Heh) and the two makifim23, Chaya (keneged Chochmah, the yud) and Yechidah (keneged the Kotz of the yud). In terms of the kelim of Tanta, which are the kelim of course, we have three levels of teamim, elyonim emtzaim and tachtonim, just as we have with nekudot. We have three tagin: some have none (i.e. they got all the ohr of ozen), some have one (i.e. are chaser from ozen but still got in the splash zone of chotem and peh), and some have three (i.e. chaser from all three orot achaf). We also have three font sizes of otiot, like the big ayin in shemah or the small alef in vayikra. We also know that each kli has three prakim, perek elyon perek emtza perek tachton, three thirds. This is why you’ll find measurements used like the shlish elyon of Tiferet from garon to chaze, or the shlish emtzai of Tiferet from chaze to tabur, or the shlish tachton of Tiferet, from tabur to Yesod. The body itself is all a bechina of kli, meaning the Ohr Penimi is nichnas in the guf24 but the makif stays out. Your head is the top part of the kli, your body is the middle part, your legs are the lower part. The middle part also has separations. The upper part of the body is of a higher madrega, processing air in the lungs and beating blood, ki hadam hu hanefesh, through the guf. The middle section processes food, and the lower section is the makom of yetzia, children or otherwise. It’s the most dinim, which is why we have a klal that there is never a ptichat rechem without dam, dinim. But if we zoom out to the total person, we see that these three kelim, though arranged vertically, are related to their horizontal counterparts. Machshava is the upper kli, which is the Kav Emtzai, which is first because it begins with keter, and then we have Dibur which is the kli for machshava, that’s the Kav Smol, and then we have Ma’aseh, which is the Kav Yamin. These three kelim are the levush on the Neshama, they are kelim. You need to work on those kelim. In torah, you work on the kli of machshava, which is chochmah, which is sight and experience metabolism. Again we have the relationship of higher, the vision itself, the middle, processing and digesting i.e. binah which makes a full baby out of the Ohr, and an end which is the resultant emotions or actions that come out of yichud of perception and the way you process it. Then we have the next stage which is Dibur, a process that is more fluid and integrated. The torso is a structure that centralizes movement and makes the two arms that actually do things function as an extension of it. By the arms as well, we have the upper arm from the shoulder to the joint, from the joint to the wrist, and finally the hand. You will find the same thing by the leg. With the torso, which is the three kelim which are in the middle, keneged Kav Smol and Speech: speech is the integration of all that you want to say in a constant flow of constriction because you can only say one word at a time, and even then, you need to use words that are cut up in the heh motzaot hapeh; it’s a grueling process of gvurah. The two arms are bound to the body that constantly mediates and uses them to its central purpose. The thing to remember is that Three is the number of Relationship, because three is kelim, the interface (mamshak) that allows for opening a field of contact25.

The instances of three can go on, and ought to go on, but there is something sorely missing. So, to once again return, we asked what the Mishnah is telling us, and we found that there are three kavin in the universal anatomy which manifest at least in the Olam of the individual as three irreducible axes of relationship. The trouble is that the anatomy sketched is, as we said, partial. We recognized that three is the anatomy that stands an Olam up, but when we consider Amidah, and its situation in a cluster of Life and Completion, positioned in opposition to the cluster of Death and Nefilah, clearly we are missing something. This picture describes the blueprint of a body, but remember that the body was coming to address something much bigger, the Olam and life itself! What happened to those themes? What is this bigger picture in which the anatomy slots in and does work to make life happen?

The Mishnah as we see it is sketched on a two-dimensional surface. These three kavin are not simply relationships but the three balls of yarn from which narrative is woven, personal narrative, horizontal interpersonal narrative, vertical narrative. There are trillions of these threads moving in each microsecond, every individual in motion in their dynamic life, embedded with others and of course in HaMakom, a space of Memale Kol Almin. It’s hard to fathom but everything that has taken place on the dry soil of earth is a step within a narrative process along one of these three threads, and often all three at once. These threads weave together, and what emerges is the thick twist of cable that is Yisrael through decision space toward Geulah across all time. What the Mishnah omits, therefore, is the Z axis26.

Earlier we uncovered the fact that underlying the twin states of Amidah and Nefilah, which these three spools of thread are concerned with, are no less than the polarities of Life and Death. It turns out that the making of a civilization built on the foundational pillars of relationship progresses from being in a state of Nefilah to a state of Amidah, and that the progress of time consists of relational dynamics, nothing more or less than that. The end of the process will therefore be a terminal state of relationship between all the elements that compose the whole of the Nivrah. But now that we have the basic shape, that the Nivrah is a whole, yet incomplete, thrust into this alienated world and forced to rebuild completeness through relationship, arriving at the original state of wholeness at the end of time, we need to look at the rod around which this cord is bound, the spine of temporal locomotion. Meaning to say, let’s step back and draw lines through the macroscope of narrative that we can then use to zoom back in to the pixel-scale microscope of individual relationships.

Let’s take stock of the numbers as they have emerged. From a world of One that remains One, there is introduced an Other, a Two, and that Two is the Nivrah i.e. Nukvah. That Two implies a Three, which is the space in which the Two relate, and is the bechinah of Relationship, which is the substance of that space in a world of pure information. But three is not only the three kavin that share a single two-dimensional plane; three is also the three points in time, Haya, Hove and Yihye. The world Was in a state; it finds itself no longer in that state and is forced to undergo a process, and at the end of that process, we have Yihye, the world that will be, the world now becoming, but always equally alive in Being, Havaya, Who never left the Chalal. Yihye, you will notice, is Yud Kei Yud Kei, which is the product at the end of the process. That means that the process has to do with a change from Yud Kei Vav Kei to Yud Kei Yud Kei, and that implies that the before state that will be returned to in Yihye was Haya, i.e. was a state of Yud Kei Yud Kei. That implies of course that the process is defined by a return.

Shabbat, you will find, is related to shav, return. Shabbat punctuates the briah at three points, three shabbatot that mark the three points in all time. There is the Shabbat of Bereshit, for we know everyone holds that the world was created on Shabbat. This Shabbat is the polarity of Zachar, it is the holiday of Existence and Reality, which is the perception of the world as overwhelmingly real, real to the exclusion of us, because we are blinded by the light of Zachrut. This is Zecher LeMa’aseh Bereshit. We then have the Shabbat of Mashiach, which is when the Kli is complete, when the Nekevah is able to return to the Zachar, and fully look the Zachar in the face, and behold the Eye Contact of Haya with the new kelim of Yihye, where Yud Kei can be brought now fully into Yud Kei. This is the right and left, Zachar and Nekevah. But there is always a third, which is the process of relationship, the drama of those kelim being made. Then there is the Shabbat of Matan Torah, for all hold that the Torah was given on Shabbat. This is a marriage document, a Ketubah. This is Zecher LeYetziat Mitzrayim, when Kudsha Brich Hu recognized the Nukvah was still around, still alive, and still committed to the dream of life, at which point He saved her from the clutches of Mitzrayim and brought her under the chupah of Sinai. The Kav Emtzai is the makom of yichud between Zachar and Nekevah, and the dual throughlines of time’s narrative that the spools of micro relationship weave into, Zecher LeMa’aseh Bereshit and Zecher LeYetziat Mitzrayim, form the duality of Zachar and Nekevah respectively, finding unification in the storybook of Hove on the road to the happily ever after of Yihye. The careful reader will note that Bereshit is reshit, rosh, and Matan Torah, being the pinnacle achievement of the middle two thousand years of history (the three being the alpaim tohu, alpaim torah and alpaim mashiach), forms the toch, and the sof hayamim, the Geulah, is of course the sof, such that bereshit torah and mashiach, tohu torah mashiach and the corresponding shabbatot, make up the rosh toch sof in the kli of history, just as we have three kelim wherever kelim are found.

The process is not to produce something new; it is a shift in what is into something old, something that was. It is not point A to point B; it is point A going round the circle and re-arriving at point A, the origin point of the circle, but different now that the journey through the circle has been experienced. That journey needs to change something for the return to Haya in Yihye to be different than the Haya which led to the need for Hove, the process. Somehow, there is a shift in our ability to relate to Havaya in Haya that requires the return process of Hove to get to a Yihye that is the same location as Haya but now different, not congruent with the situation of Yud Kei Yud Kei that became Yud Kei Vav Kei. And if the lifting up of the world to return to a place of Yud Kei Yud Kei, healed from whatever was missing in the Haya of Yud Kei Vav Kei, must be accomplished through the three kavin, then we need to clarify in practice what engine drives the contextual push for activity in olam haze in light of the matrix we have set up.

The locomotion of reality is through an engine of Teshuvah, which is to say, perud pulled into yichud, returned to yichud, because yichud was always the situation of reality at its truest. Teshuvah is Shabbat, and Adam HaRishon wrote a song on Shabbat when he, i.e. we, was allowed back home for a day. He said, mizmor shir leyom hashavat, the day of return. What is Shabbat? It is the day that the six days of the week lead into, which the six days of the week construct. Sheshet yamim taavod veasita kol melachtecha, the sheshet yeme hamaase are days of ma’aseh, days where we make the world. Shabbat is the day we live in the world we have made. Every Shabbat, you enter as if everything is perfect, because you have reached the perfection of that cycle. Nothing more needs doing. Shabbat is Heh Achrona. On Rishon, Sheni and Shelishi leShabbat, we build Yud Kei Vav, while on Revi’i, Chamishi, and Shishi, we build Alef Heh Yud. Where are the last letters, the Nukvah of the two shemot Havaya Ekye? Shabbat is the Nukvah, it is the circular modality that completes the Zachrut of sheshet yeme hamaase, six days, Chagat Nahi, Za, Baala, the Husband of Shabbat Malketa. Mi Melech malchei hamlachim, Kudsha Brich Hu, as we sing every Friday night, Hakara in the Kli of Nukvah.

Did you notice what happened? We built a Shem. Teshuvah is synonymous with building a Shem. Are we all that surprised that the entire narrative of time boils down in mechanism to building a Shem, once we already know that a Shem, like all otiot, is a kli, and the one unified Shem of the entire Briah is Nukvah, besod bayom hahu Yihye Havaya Echad Ushmo Echad, the zivug of Kav Emtzai? We are not surprised. We are eager, eager because the follow-up question begs to be asked. We wanted to know how to ma’amid the Olam, because Amidah is life, and life is the plot of reality, because to be Davuk and beAchdut Gamur is to be fully alive, with kelim that can hold maximal life. We then learned that the universal anatomy of the Briah is built for this function of revival, Amidah, and is expressed in three kelim, Yamin Smol Emtzai, Rosh Toch Sof, a matrix of 9, the Tas that builds malchut, the Kli, the Nekevah, of Shabbat, the Shabbat that is the completion of the shemot, which is the Nekevah, causing us now to demand: what is this inyan of building shemot? Why is building shemot the secret of all Avodat HaShem? How does building shemot provide the context for all reality as an Avodah, regardless of how ‘mundane’ the particularities might seem to you? What are shemot anyways? Might shemot have to do with the atomic level of the universe’s construction, which is to suggest that shemot perhaps compose primary reality? Hold on to these questions, because the Chochmah of Atzilut educates the wise in the secret of shemot, and once one knows the secret of shemot, one can understand just about anything you want.

But in linear algebra, we learn to intuit reality where we find multiple dimensions of information within a single object. A person is many things, for example. They consume food, so there is a dimension of hunger, they can locomote if they have legs, so there is a dimension of speed etc. If you ask a person a question, say, ‘Are you hungry?’, that is asking them to give you data within one dimension, but in truth this is a multidimensional being. A vector is a mathematical object that holds data in multiple dimensions. Dimensions of information are the anatomy of an object, and the data within those sockets make up its identity.
